title: Framer or a production codebase
excerpt: Framer is a fast way to design a marketing site in the browser. A Next.js codebase is the right home when the site must share a system with the product.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky, separate structures that still have to share one system.
caption: Separate buildings against one sky. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is Framer enough for the marketing site?
faqs.answer: Framer is enough when the site is a set of marketing pages, the product lives elsewhere, and the people who edit are not waiting on engineers. It is also a good place to try a headline before you commit a build. You still need a small discipline so buttons and type do not drift.

faqs.question: When should the marketing site live in a Next.js codebase?
faqs.answer: Put it in the codebase when it must share components or tokens with the product, when engineers will be the ones maintaining it, or when the page has states a canvas will flatten. The company should own the repository and the hosting account. Copy still needs an editing path, or the site will go stale.

faqs.question: Can you design in Framer and build in code?
faqs.answer: Yes. The design file is where you try the sentence, and the codebase is where the sentence becomes the site you keep. Trouble starts when both are live and each has a different headline. Pick one source of truth.

markdown:
Framer vs next.js is a choice about where the marketing site should live. Framer is a fast way to design a marketing site in the browser and publish it. A Next.js codebase is the right home when the site must share a system with a product, or when engineers are the people who will keep it.

Hanabi uses both kinds of tools for what they are. Framer is a design tool in the studio. Production sites are built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The mistake is to treat that stack preference as a rule for every founder. The rule is the editing path and the shared system.

## What Framer is for

Framer lets you design with the real type, the real width, and a publish button. For a marketing site with a handful of pages, that loop is fast. You see the mobile frame while you write the headline. You do not wait for a handoff to find out the line breaks badly.

Use it when the site is the marketing site and the product lives somewhere else. A waitlist, an offer, a few landing pages, a journal if you will truly write it. The people editing are designers or founders, and they want to change a section without opening a repository.

Framer is also a good place to try a headline before you commit a sprint to it. A day in the tool can answer whether the first screen makes sense. You can throw the attempt away. That is cheaper than a week of component work for a sentence you will replace.

The limit is the same as any builder. The site becomes a set of pages with their own styles unless someone is strict. A component you meant to reuse gets detached and edited in one place. Six months later the buttons disagree. If you stay in Framer, you need a small discipline: text styles, colors, and a few components you do not detach. The tool will not enforce that for you.

Publishing from the tool is a feature. It is also a boundary. The marketing site and the product will not share a deploy, a type scale, or a set of tokens unless you manually keep them in step. For many early companies that is acceptable. Say so in the open, so nobody expects the app and the site to match by magic.

## What a codebase is for

A production codebase is for a site that engineers will run, and for pages that must stay aligned with the product. Next.js on Vercel, with React and TypeScript, is a common shape because the product is often already there. Tailwind keeps the styling in the components. Motion is available when a transition has to be part of the interface, with a reduced-motion path.

Choose this home when at least one of these is true:

- The marketing site and the product share components, tokens, or copy that must not drift.
- Engineers are the people who will change the site, and they want review, preview deploys, and a history.
- The page has states a canvas will oversimplify: account-aware content, a real configurator, content from your own database.
- You need to meet a performance bar by editing the actual loading path.

Prisma and PostgreSQL belong in this picture only when the site has real records: accounts, posts, a catalog with rules. A brochure does not need a database. Adding one because the stack diagram looked complete is how a simple site becomes an operations problem.

The cost is the editing path. Someone has to make copy changes possible for the people who should make them. That might be a small CMS, a pull request the founder does not fear, or a portal where the finished files and the updates live. If you do not design that path, the site will be correct and stale. Engineers will be asked to change a headline, and they will resent it, and the headline will wait.

## One system with the product

The strongest reason to put the site in the codebase is a shared system. The product already has a type ramp, a color, a button, a way of writing the offer. The site should use those, or the company looks like two companies.

Got Next and Leadly, public Hanabi product interfaces, are the kind of work where this matters. The interface is the product. A marketing page that imitates it in another tool will be wrong the next time the product team adjusts a label. Building the page in the same React components, or in tokens that both sides import, keeps the promise the screenshot makes.

Trade Moai, a trading interface concept, makes the same point in miniature. A concept can live in a design file. The moment it is a site people visit, the frames and the build have to agree. Two sources of truth is how a concept starts to look like a costume of itself.

You can still design in Framer or Figma and build in Next.js. That is a normal studio path. The design file is where you try the sentence. The codebase is where the sentence becomes the site. The failure mode is publishing the design file as the site and also maintaining a product, then acting surprised when they diverge.

Shared system does not mean the marketing page is a screenshot of the app. It means the offer, the type, and the components that repeat are the same decisions. The page can be quieter than the product. It should not be a different brand.

## Who edits it next year

Ask who will change a paragraph in eleven months. If the answer is the founder, and there is no engineer on staff, Framer is the kinder home. If the answer is an engineer who already ships the product, the codebase is the kinder home. If the answer is "we will hire someone," you are guessing. Decide for the team you have.

Write the edit list. Headline, price, a new landing page, a logo swap, a post. Mark which of those a non-engineer must be able to do. Then look at the tool. If the must-do list is all inside Framer's editor, stay. If the must-do list includes a behavior Framer will embed from somewhere else, you have already chosen a codebase and added a toy.

Billing and access are part of editing. The company should own the Framer project and the Vercel team. A studio login as the only admin is a loan. The handoff includes the admin role, the domain, and a short note on how to publish. On a Hanabi project, the client portal is where brand files, docs, and updates live after delivery. That is the operational half of ownership. The tool choice is the other half.

## Motion and measurement

Motion is where Framer feels like the point. You can make a page move quickly, in the same place you design it. Use that for a marketing page when the motion explains something: a panel, a sequence of the product, a transition that keeps context. Cut it when it delays the offer.

In a codebase, Motion can do the same job with one advantage: you can honor a reduced-motion preference as part of the component, and you can keep the animation off the first paint. The page should still say the offer if the animation never runs. That is the test, in either tool.

Performance is the other test, and it should be the same test in both homes. [web.dev's Core Web Vitals guide](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) documents the metrics: largest contentful paint, interaction to next paint, and cumulative layout shift. The good thresholds are an LCP within 2.5 seconds, an INP within 200 milliseconds, and a CLS under 0.1. A Framer marketing page can hit those. A Next.js page can miss them. Measure the one you will publish, on a phone, with real images.

If the only reason you are leaving Framer is a score you have not measured, stay and measure. If you have measured, and the tool's runtime is the reason you cannot get the hero stable or the page responsive, that is a fact. Move the site, or simplify the page until the tool can carry it.

## What you take with you

Leaving Framer means the visual system has to be rebuilt or carefully exported. Type styles, colors, and the actual copy are the assets. Absolute-positioned frames are not a design system. Before you publish a Framer site you might later rebuild, keep the copy in a document and the decisions in a short list: type, color, spacing, the components you repeat. Illustrator or Figma can hold the mark. The pages should not be the only place the logo exists.

Leaving a codebase means the next team inherits a repository. Make it ordinary. A readme with the install, the environment, and the deploy. No secret in the git history. Components named for what they are. A founder should be able to point a new engineer at the repo and expect a local page within an hour, assuming the engineer already knows Next.js.

You can use Framer for design exploration and Next.js for the site you will keep. You can use Framer as the site until the product and the site must share a system, then move. Both sequences are coherent. The incoherent one is two live marketing sites, each with a different headline, because nobody decided which one was the source.

Templates are the broader version of this trap. A template can be right when the offer is ordinary, and wrong when its sections invent a company you are not. That choice is next: [template or a designed site](/blog/template-or-a-designed-site).

If you are sorting a marketing site from a product codebase and want a studio to hold both the design and the build, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services).
